title: Correcting Data Types knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which practice is most closely aligned with “Correcting Data Types” and its subtopic “Numeric conversion”?
options: Choose the most complex available method even when a simpler baseline answers the question.
Use numeric conversion in service of the stated question, then check evidence and assumptions.
Treat a strong result on the examples used to tune the method as proof it will generalize.
Skip input checks whenever the first output appears plausible.
questions.answer_key: Use numeric conversion in service of the stated question, then check evidence and assumptions.
questions.explanation: The curriculum connects correcting data types with numeric conversion. Apply the relevant method to a defined question and check the evidence and assumptions instead of overgeneralizing from one example.

questions.prompt: Before you rely on a result related to “Correcting Data Types”, what is the strongest next step?
options: Tune decisions against the final test set until the score reaches the desired level.
Assume the same method will work across all populations, locations, and time periods.
Check input quality and units, compare with an expected or baseline result, and record limitations.
Check only whether the code completed without an error.
questions.answer_key: Check input quality and units, compare with an expected or baseline result, and record limitations.
questions.explanation: Validate input quality and units, compare the result to an appropriate expectation or baseline, and record the limits. This is particularly important when working with dates and timestamps.

questions.prompt: A small example of “Correcting Data Types” works as expected. What does that establish?
options: It proves a causal mechanism for every population and time period.
It guarantees fairness, privacy, security, and accuracy without a separate review.
It removes the need for documentation, testing, or monitoring.
Treat success as limited evidence; check representative cases, uncertainty, and real-world risks before relying on it.
questions.answer_key: Treat success as limited evidence; check representative cases, uncertainty, and real-world risks before relying on it.
questions.explanation: A small example supports only a limited claim under its tested conditions. Generalization requires representative evidence, uncertainty analysis where relevant, and review of real-world risks.
